design_detail: Qualitative interview study (Harm Reduct J 2022;19:4; open access, CC BY), the qualitative component of a larger sequential mixed-methods study of methamphetamine use in Nevada and New Mexico. 21 loosely structured interviews, December 2019 to February 2020, with people aged 18 or over who reported using methamphetamine in the previous 3 months, recruited by street and agency outreach and chain referral. Four questions concerned negative experiences and overdose: drawbacks and negative experiences; whether the respondent or anyone they knew had experienced what they believed to be a methamphetamine overdose and what it looked or felt like; experiences of seeking medical care; and strategies used to reduce harms. Interviews were recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed inductively (thematic analysis) by a single analyst, with team discussion of memos and codes and a second researcher joining for the final organization of themes. No tables or figures; findings are presented as themes with quoted extracts labelled by respondent number, ethnicity, race, sex, age band, state and drugs used.
can_establish: How these 21 people described, in their own terms, what happens when too much methamphetamine is taken ('overamping'), how they distinguished it from opioid overdose, what they did about it, and what help they found when they sought care.
cannot_establish: How common any of these experiences is, whether methamphetamine rather than sleep deprivation or other drugs caused them, whether route of administration changes the risk (the authors say explicitly that their data cannot be used for this), or how often fatal methamphetamine overdose occurs; a purposive sample of 21 people in two states supports none of these.

sample.recruitment: Street and agency-based outreach in both states (flyers and one-to-one outreach at encampments of people experiencing homelessness, syringe service programmes and bars) plus chain referral through existing participants. Community partners (public health authorities, treatment providers, harm reduction agencies) took part in design and gave access to their premises. Interviews took place in private or semi-private settings, including partner offices, encampments and participants' dwellings. Participants were paid 40 US dollars immediately after consent, and reminded they could stop at any time, to limit any sense of coercion.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: age 18 or over and self-reported methamphetamine use in the past 3 months. All interviews were conducted in English, although Spanish was offered. No exclusion criteria are reported.
sample.demographics: 48% female and 52% male; 2 participants Black, 10 White, 3 multiracial, 6 Latinx; median age 35 years (IQR 30 to 43); 48% homeless; 81% had completed 12 or more years of education; 38% employed full or part time.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). The number approached or declining is not reported, and no saturation criterion is given for stopping at 21 interviews.
sample.selection_effects: Named by the authors: a convenience sample recruited where many people experiencing homelessness are found, from two western states with high rates of methamphetamine and opioid deaths, so findings may not transfer to people with more stable housing or to other regions. In addition, 17 of 21 also used opioids, so the sample is not of people who use methamphetamine alone; people who had died of an overdose are by definition absent, which bears directly on the central finding that fatal overdose was said to be rare.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in interview; no toxicology, no quantification of amount or frequency, and no instrument. Eligibility was self-reported use within 3 months.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured. 'Overconsumption' is the respondents' own notion, not a quantity. Respondents repeatedly tied symptoms to runs of two to three days without sleep rather than to an amount. Route was not asked about systematically; the paper reports that nearly half the sample named injecting as making delusions and hallucinations more likely, and gives accounts of people changing route afterwards.
exposure.polysubstance: Central and not controllable: 17 of 21 used opioids (heroin, methadone or prescription opioids) as well as methamphetamine, and all but two quoted extracts are labelled 'MA+heroin' or 'MA+methadone'. Alcohol was not asked about systematically; of the four respondents who described memory lapses, two said they drank and one had cut down. The authors state that symptoms could be due to sleep deprivation or other substances rather than methamphetamine itself.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; no requirement of abstinence and no account of intoxication at interview.

comparison.controls: None (qualitative design). Comparison is internal and conceptual: respondents contrasted methamphetamine 'overamping' with opioid overdose, and one contrasted methamphetamine paranoia (after days awake) with cocaine paranoia (immediate).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No information on psychiatric history, prior psychosis, sleep disorders or medical comorbidity, any of which bears on the symptoms described.

outcomes.instruments: A loosely structured interview guide with four overdose-related questions (reproduced in the Methods) plus a short demographic questionnaire. Analysis was inductive thematic coding with a hierarchical code scheme; no software, coding frame, saturation assessment, member checking or reporting checklist (such as COREQ) is named.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. Credibility rests on team discussion of memos and codes, involvement of researchers and service providers including people with lived and living experience of substance use, and illustrative quotation.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Overdose' was left to the respondents to define, which is the point of the study; the authors group what respondents described into psychological and physical symptoms and appraise each for desirability, discomfort, concern about health or safety, and perceived need for emergency care.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; a single analyst coded all transcripts, with the research team discussing and refining codes.

analysis.effect_sizes: None, and none would be appropriate: this is a thematic analysis without quantitative comparison. The only counts reported are descriptive: 2 of 21 interviews containing an account of an apparently fatal methamphetamine overdose (both second-hand and apparently the same event), 17 of 21 using opioids as well, 4 of 21 describing memory lapses, and 'nearly half' naming injecting as raising the chance of hallucinations.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol registration or published analysis plan is mentioned; approval was by the University of Nevada, Reno institutional review board, with the University of New Mexico deferring under a single-IRB agreement.
analysis.selective_reporting: Quotations are attributed to respondent identifiers, so the reader can see that several themes rest on the same few people (for example R8, R10 and R14 each appear three times); the number of respondents endorsing each theme is usually not given. Full transcripts are not available because of the sensitivity of the content; redacted excerpts can be requested through the university's research integrity office.
analysis.power: Not applicable. No sampling target or saturation criterion is stated for the 21 interviews.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this group, acute fatal methamphetamine overdose was described as rare or, by some, impossible; what respondents described instead was 'overamping', a continuum of psychological symptoms (memory lapses, anxiety, paranoia, delusions, hallucinations, some experienced as spiritual and some as terrifying) and physical symptoms (an overwhelming urge to sleep, pounding heart, uncontrollable 'flailing'), usually attributed by respondents to several days awake without food or water rather than to the drug itself; medical care was rarely sought and, when sought, was experienced as having little to offer.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions stay close to this, which is the strength of the paper: the authors say explicitly that their respondents claimed fatal overdose is rare or impossible, that symptoms may be due to sleep deprivation or polysubstance use rather than methamphetamine, and that their findings should not be used to draw conclusions about routes of administration or combinations. Two small stretches: the Results report that nearly half the sample identified injecting as increasing the chance of delusions and hallucinations, a quantified statement derived from a question that was not systematically asked (the limitations acknowledge this); and the limitations state that respondents were asked specifically about witnessing fatal methamphetamine overdoses, whereas the question printed in the Methods asks whether they or anyone they knew had experienced what they believed to be an overdose. The Discussion's policy proposals (overdose prevention sites, drug checking, safer supply) go beyond what 21 interviews can support, and are offered as directions rather than findings.

timeline.event: Darke, Kaye & Duflou: 7-year Australian national study of methamphetamine-related deaths, cited here as background (toxicology detected other substances in 83% of cases and methamphetamine toxicity alone was the cause in 6.1%; 1649 deaths)

Wagner, Chase, Anderson, Reyes, Harding, Fiuty & Page: survey of 420 people who use drugs in the same two states, from the same programme of work, comparing self-reported symptoms of acute methamphetamine toxicity with opioid and mixed overdose (Acad Emerg Med 33(1):e70217; not read for this card)

replication.where_it_stands: The standard qualitative reference for how people who use methamphetamine describe 'overamping', widely cited for the claim that methamphetamine overdose does not fit the opioid overdose template. It should be cited for the description and the vocabulary, never for frequency. The same group's 2026 survey of 420 people is the quantitative successor and is the place to look for symptom proportions; the two are not independent, sharing authors, sites and programme.

funding.funder: Clinical Translational Research Infrastructure Network, grant 5U54GM104944-07 (a US National Institute of General Medical Sciences award).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors and research staff declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: School of Public Health, University of Nevada, Reno; University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center; and The Mountain Center Harm Reduction Center, Santa Fe (one author is a harm reduction service provider). The research team is described as including people with lived and living experience of substance use, which is a strength for interpretation and is declared.

what_would_settle_it: For frequency and clinical meaning: a prospective study in which people who use methamphetamine record symptom episodes as they happen, with contemporaneous measurement of sleep, other substances taken and, where possible, physiological measures, so that the contributions of methamphetamine, sleep deprivation and polysubstance use can be separated; linked to emergency-department and toxicology data so that the described continuum can be mapped onto clinically recognizable events.

domains.domain: Research design appropriate to the question (qualitative appraisal, CASP-style)
domains.note: The question is how people define and experience methamphetamine overdose; interviews are the right method and the four questions are printed in full.

Convenience and chain-referral sampling in outreach settings; no account of how many were approached or declined, no sampling frame and no saturation criterion for stopping at 21. People who died are necessarily absent from a sample used to characterize fatal overdose as rare.

Trained interviewers, loosely structured guide, private or semi-private settings, recorded and transcribed verbatim, English only with Spanish offered; interview setting varied (offices, encampments, dwellings), which may affect candour.

Team composition including service providers and people with lived experience is stated, but there is no reflexive account of interviewer characteristics or of how the analyst's position shaped the coding.

IRB approval with a single-IRB agreement, written informed consent, immediate payment to avoid coercion, de-identification and an explicit consent-for-publication statement; transcripts withheld for participant protection.

Inductive thematic analysis by a single coder with team discussion; no independent double coding, no member checking, no negative-case analysis described, no software or audit trail named, and no reporting checklist (COREQ) cited.
Themes are illustrated with attributed extracts and the authors state alternative explanations (sleep deprivation, alcohol, polysubstance use) for their own findings.
Limitations state plainly that the findings may not generalize beyond these communities and must not be used to draw conclusions about routes, substances or combinations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised as a qualitative study, not with an effect-estimate instrument: no risk-of-bias tool in the schema applies, so CASP-style domains are used. The design, ethics and grounding are sound and the authors are unusually explicit about what their data cannot show. The limits are a convenience sample of 21 with no saturation account, single-coder analysis without independent double coding or member checking, and the inseparability of methamphetamine from opioids and sleep deprivation in nearly every account. The findings are credible as descriptions of how these people understand overamping, and carry no information about frequency.

key_findings.finding: 21 people were interviewed (11 Nevada, 10 New Mexico); 17 of 21 used opioids as well as methamphetamine and only 4 used methamphetamine alone. Median age 35 (IQR 30 to 43); 48% female; 48% homeless; 81% with 12 or more years of education; 38% employed.

Asked whether they or anyone they knew had experienced a methamphetamine overdose, respondents said acute fatal overdose was rare and some said it was not possible. Only 2 of the 21 interviews contained an account of an apparently fatal methamphetamine overdose; both were second-hand and appear to describe the same event, with sparse detail except that the person was left alone. In the other 19, respondents described non-life-threatening psychological or physical effects of taking too much.

Respondents used 'overamping' rather than 'overdose' for these experiences, describing them on a continuum from less to more severe and, in several accounts, as the body shutting down or switching off from overstimulation rather than as a life-threatening event.
key_findings.locator: Results › Experiences of overdose, 2nd–3rd paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Psychiatric effects formed a continuum: memory lapses (described by 4 respondents, with gaps of days and sudden onset, likened to alcohol blackouts, with no falls or injuries reported but one respondent naming vulnerability to sexual assault while in that state), then anxiety, then paranoia, delusions and hallucinations, which often occurred together.

Hallucinations were interpreted in opposite ways: some respondents described them as welcome or spiritual, others as terrifying (one describing an attack by the devil, another a delusion of having killed someone that led to hospital transport and continuing auditory hallucinations of staff conspiring to kill him). Most respondents read these symptoms as a signal to sleep rather than as a reason to seek care.

When care was sought (emergency department, 911 or community providers), respondents described finding that little could be done beyond waiting it out in a safe place; one quoted account has a community programme saying they did not know how to address methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychiatric effects, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nearly half the sample said injecting, compared with other routes, made delusions and hallucinations more likely; some described stopping injecting and smoking instead after a frightening episode. The authors note this was not asked systematically and state in the limitations that their findings must not be used to draw conclusions about routes of administration.
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychiatric effects, 9th–11th paragraphs; Discussion › limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Physical effects reported: an overwhelming urge to sleep (described as the body turning off, with waking either refreshed or hungover, and not as fainting); cardiovascular sensations, one respondent describing a feeling that his heart would burst through his chest, alarming at the time but believed to pass, as it did; and 'flailing', uncontrollable rapid movements of arms, legs or jaw, unpleasant and sometimes frightening but rarely seen as a health emergency, with some respondents' main concern being that it showed others they were using.

Respondents attributed these symptoms mainly to the cumulative effect of being awake for days while using, with dehydration and not eating, rather than to the drug as such; symptoms typically appeared after two to three days awake, and for some this signalled the need to rest and stop for a while. One respondent contrasted methamphetamine paranoia (after days awake) with cocaine paranoia (immediately after the first use).
key_findings.locator: Results › The role of sleep deprivation, dehydration, and hunger

key_findings.finding: Strategies available to respondents were general self-care: sleeping, drinking water, eating. One respondent described giving other people an over-the-counter antihistamine or milk for cardiac symptoms; the authors note that clinical guidance for such use is lacking. Several could name no clinical or harm reduction option at all, mirroring what they found when they sought medical care.
key_findings.locator: Results › The role of sleep deprivation...; Discussion, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Reported as what respondents said they did, not as a practice with evidence behind it; the paper states there is no equivalent of naloxone for methamphetamine.

key_findings.finding: The authors' framing: methamphetamine overdose may not fit the opioid template, since opioid death follows respiratory depression, while methamphetamine-related death involves cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease and polysubstance use; they cite an Australian 7-year autopsy study in which other substances were detected in 83% of methamphetamine-related deaths and methamphetamine toxicity alone was the cause in 6.1% of 1649 deaths.
key_findings.note: The Australian figures are second-hand background (Darke, Kaye & Duflou 2017); the citation marked [16] in that passage gives the 2017 Addiction paper.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the symptoms described could be caused by extreme sleep deprivation (which is known to produce hallucinations and to raise anxiety and depression risk) or by polysubstance use rather than by the acute effects of methamphetamine, and that their design cannot separate these.

reporting_issues.issue: The same respondent identifier is given different age bands: R8 appears as 'Female, 30 s' in one extract and 'Female, 20s' in two others; R13's second extract omits the age band present in the first.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but quote attributions cannot be relied on to count distinct respondents by age; anyone recounting these extracts should cite the identifier only.

reporting_issues.issue: Race and ethnicity are reported inconsistently: the Results give mutually exclusive counts (2 Black, 10 White, 3 multiracial, 6 Latinx, totalling 21), while quote attributions code ethnicity and race separately, so that respondents appear as 'Hispanic/Latino, Black' or 'Hispanic/Latina, White'.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 6 Latinx cannot be mapped onto the racial categories; the sample's composition cannot be reconstructed exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations state that respondents were asked specifically about witnessing fatal methamphetamine overdoses; the interview question printed in the Methods asks whether the respondent or anyone they knew had experienced what they believed to be a methamphetamine overdose.
reporting_issues.consequence: The central negative finding rests on a broader question than the limitations describe; it is about what respondents believed to be overdoses, not about witnessed deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results quantify that nearly half the sample named injecting as increasing the chance of delusions and hallucinations, although the paper says route was not asked about systematically, and the limitations then forbid conclusions about route.
reporting_issues.consequence: The proportion comes from unprompted mentions and understates nothing but means nothing as a rate; it must not be cited as a route comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: Analysis details that bear on credibility are missing: no software, no saturation criterion for 21 interviews, no independent double coding, no member checking and no COREQ or similar checklist, although a single analyst coded all transcripts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Standard qualitative reporting items are absent; the themes cannot be audited beyond the quoted extracts.

reporting_issues.issue: The author contributions list initials 'PH' for a contribution, while the author list contains Phillip Fiuty (PF) and no author with those initials; one contributor email address is given as a 'umn.edu' address for an author affiliated with the University of New Mexico.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the findings.

reporting_issues.issue: Interviews were conducted December 2019 to February 2020 and published in January 2022, before the period of steepest increase in methamphetamine-involved deaths involving fentanyl that the Discussion addresses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Accounts predate the later fentanyl-contamination picture; the fentanyl-in-methamphetamine figures quoted in the Discussion (0.1% of US seizures in 2016; 5.9% of 15 samples at one Vancouver site in 2017–2018) are second-hand and older still.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8762891 (published open-access version; all sections including every quoted extract with its attribution, limitations, acknowledgements, author contributions, funding, data-availability, ethics, consent and competing-interests statements and author affiliations; the article has no tables or figures; the reference list was read in part, to reference 20, which covers the sources cited for the background figures used in this card; no supplementary material)
